summary: Describes a way to mix a preshared key into the IKEv2 key exchange so VPN traffic stays protected even if quantum computers later break today's key exchange. It addresses the risk of someone recording VPN traffic now and decrypting it later.

plainLanguage.summary: Even if someone records secret messages now, a shared secret password mixed into the key keeps them safe from future super-computers.

questions: how to make ikev2 post-quantum secure
what is ikev2 preshared key mixing
what is a ppk in ikev2
should i use a group ppk
subtitle: Mixing an extra preshared key into IKEv2 so VPN traffic resists future quantum computers.

tldr.problem: A quantum computer could solve the Diffie-Hellman problems IKEv2 relies on, so someone storing VPN traffic today could decrypt it later.
tldr.mechanism: Both peers hold an extra Post-quantum Preshared Key (PPK) and stir it into the IKEv2 keys SK_d, SK_pi and SK_pr, using three new notifications to agree on it.
tldr.outcome: Child SA keys and later IKE SAs become quantum secure if the PPK has enough entropy, while the rest of IKEv2 stays unchanged.

today: RFC 8784 is a Proposed Standard from June 2020. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: The Quantum Problem and the Idea
sections.content:
A quantum computer would be able to solve Diffie-Hellman (DH) and Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman problems in polynomial time, which would compromise existing IKEv2 systems. IKEv1 with strong preshared keys is not vulnerable, because those keys are an input to key derivation.

RFC 8784 gives IKEv2 a similar property. An additional secret shared by initiator and responder is stirred into SK_d, which feeds Child SA keys and later IKE SAs, and into SK_pi and SK_pr, which lets both sides detect a mismatch cleanly. Existing authentication and (EC)DH stay in place; they are strengthened, not replaced.
sections.plainLanguage: The old lock could be picked by a future machine. Adding a secret both friends already know makes the lock safe again.

sections.title: Assumptions
sections.content: Each peer has a list of Post-quantum Preshared Keys (PPKs) with identifiers (PPK_ID), and the initiator chooses which PPK to use with a given responder. A configurable flag says whether using the PPK is mandatory. The PPK is separate from any preshared key IKEv2 uses for authentication, because that one is not used for key derivation. Per peer, the configuration is the tuple Peer, PPK, PPK_ID, mandatory_or_not.
sections.plainLanguage: Each friend keeps a list of secret passwords and a note saying whether the password is required.

sections.title: The Exchanges
sections.content:
If the initiator is configured to use a PPK, it MUST include a USE_PPK notification (type 16435) in the IKE_SA_INIT request. A responder that does not support PPKs or has none configured ignores it. Otherwise it answers with its own USE_PPK. If the responder does not, and the PPK is mandatory, the initiator MUST abort; if optional, it continues as normal IKEv2.

The initiator then derives the keys and in IKE_AUTH sends a PPK_IDENTITY notification (type 16436) carrying the PPK_ID. If PPK use is optional it MUST also include NO_PPK_AUTH (type 16437), holding authentication data computed without the PPK, so a responder lacking that PPK can still proceed. If the responder does not know the PPK_ID and PPKs are mandatory or no NO_PPK_AUTH was sent, it MUST send AUTHENTICATION_FAILED. When it uses the PPK, the responder replies with an empty PPK_IDENTITY.

With EAP, the responder's first AUTH payload is computed without the PPK because it does not yet know the PPK_ID.
sections.plainLanguage: The friends first ask whether both have a secret. If so, one tells the other which secret by its label, never the secret itself.

sections.title: How the Keys Are Mixed
sections.content:
The standard IKEv2 derivation runs first, giving primed subkeys SK_d', SK_pi' and SK_pr'. Each is then run through prf+ again with the PPK as the key to give the final SK_d, SK_pi and SK_pr. For the PRFs defined for IKEv2, whose output size equals the preferred key size, only the first iteration is needed: prf (PPK, SK_d' | 0x01) and so on.

The PPK is used this way only during initial IKE SA setup. It MUST NOT be used when the subkeys are calculated for an IKE SA rekey, resumption or similar operations.
sections.plainLanguage: The friends first make a lock the usual way, then scramble it once more using their shared secret.

sections.title: Upgrading an Existing Network
sections.content:
The design lets administrators add PPKs without disruption. First, configure the PPKs on each node and set mandatory_or_not to false for each peer. Nodes still work with those not yet upgraded, because of USE_PPK and NO_PPK_AUTH.

Optionally, once all nodes are upgraded, mark PPK use as mandatory. This does not change strength against a passive attacker, but an active attacker with a fast enough quantum computer then cannot mount a downgrade attack.
sections.plainLanguage: You can hand out the secrets slowly. Old and new devices keep working together until everyone is ready.

sections.title: PPK Format and Management
sections.content:
The first octet of the PPK_ID is its type. PPK_ID_OPAQUE (1) has an unspecified format both sides understand, and PPK_ID_FIXED (2) uses fixed octet strings configured locally on both sides; for the latter, limiting strings to the base64 character set is recommended.

Operationally, a unique PPK per pair gives full peer authentication but does not scale. A single group PPK is NOT RECOMMENDED: members can record each other's traffic and decrypt it once they have a quantum computer, and a widely known PPK is easier to steal. PPK-only authentication is possible with the NULL Authentication method, but then PPKs MUST be mandatory, and combining it with a group PPK is NOT RECOMMENDED because any member could impersonate another.
sections.plainLanguage: Each pair of friends should have their own secret. One secret shared by a crowd is easy to leak.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The PPK must be random. The strongest practice is at least 256 bits of entropy, giving 128 bits of post-quantum security, because Grover's algorithm effectively halves a symmetric key. Deriving a PPK from a password or name is not secure.

An attacker with a quantum computer can read the initial IKE SA, including identities, configuration and traffic selectors, but not the IPsec SA keys. Deployments that send sensitive data over IKE SAs MUST rekey the IKE SA first. Policy SHOULD allow only quantum-secure symmetric algorithms; keys under 256 bits, and PRF_AES128_XCBC and PRF_AES128_CBC, are listed as providing less than 128 bits of post-quantum security.

If PPKs are optional for both peers and signatures are used, a quantum attacker can strip USE_PPK in a downgrade attack. A mandatory-PPK initiator that aborts at once on a missing USE_PPK is exposed to a forged reply, so it is RECOMMENDED to keep retransmitting until a genuine reply arrives or the exchange times out. Implementations SHOULD audit cases where a configured PPK was not used.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret must be truly random and long, not a name or a word, or guessers can win.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA registered three IKEv2 status notify types: USE_PPK (16435), PPK_IDENTITY (16436) and NO_PPK_AUTH (16437). It also created the subregistry "IKEv2 Post-quantum Preshared Key ID Types": 0 is reserved, 1 is PPK_ID_OPAQUE, 2 is PPK_ID_FIXED, 3 to 127 are unassigned (Expert Review) and 128 to 255 are for private use.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of numbers got three new entries for the new messages.

messages.label: IKE_SA_INIT + USE_PPK
messages.note: Initiator signals it wants to use a PPK.

messages.label: IKE_AUTH + PPK_IDENTITY
messages.note: Empty notification shows the PPK is used.

items.label: USE_PPK
items.desc: Signals willingness to use a PPK.

items.label: PPK_IDENTITY
items.desc: Carries the PPK_ID, or is empty in the reply.

items.label: NO_PPK_AUTH
items.desc: Authentication data computed without the PPK.
